Our party has been a vehement defender of the constitutional rights of women to be treated the same as men. By this point, we have made great progress both in addressing wage disparity and the restrictions marriage pushes upon both employed and unemployed women[? if abortion_rights: , and even pushed through a bill to legalize abortion despite the conservative opposition ?]. However, all our efforts show that it is not enough: our enemy ought to be the patriarchal culture so prevalent in Germany: without tackling this foundation, no Constitution can overcome the misogynistic sentiments entrenched this deep.
We stand together with the feminist movement.

Through Marie Juchacz's work in our Frauensekretariat, we negotiate with **Bund Deutscher Frauenvereine** to urge them to reconcile their past opposition to leftist organization, and start negotiating our further cooperation to hold extensive campaigns, promoting women's rights at work and at home, seeking to offer a common ground to both "traditional" and "new" women to incentivize their participation in social life beyond the Imperial "Kinder, Küche, Kirche". We make accent on the livelihoods of widows and mothers who have lost their family in the Great War, those women who belong to the working poor, and aim to shift the blame in the popular perception of domestic abuse from influence of alcohol to present power imbalances.

While some prominent conservative activists, like Annagrete Lehmann of [? if dnvp_ideology == "Radical": **DNVP**?][? if dnvp_ideology == "Moderate": **DNF**?], oppose our efforts out of a principle, even the most traditional women have grievances our rhetoric can appeal to.
